chapter.name: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
chapter.blurb: Theme D, Governance and Democracy: how India's Parliament is built and how it works. A school trip to the new Parliament building opens the chapter, and the Introduction sets out Universal Adult Franchise, the direct election of the Lok Sabha, and Parliament as the supreme legislative body that controls and guides the government. The Parliament is then composed -- the President with two Houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, a bicameral design chosen in the spirit of federalism, with a Speaker elected by the Lok Sabha and the Vice President chairing the Rajya Sabha. Its work is classified under four heads: constitutional functions, lawmaking, executive accountability and financial accountability. The journey of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 and a nine-step flowchart carry a bill to an act; the Question Hour, Standing Committees and the annual budget hold the Executive to account. The Union Executive -- President, Vice President and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister -- is then set beside the Legislature in a comparison table, the Judiciary is introduced as the custodian of the Constitution in a system of checks and balances, the same structure is traced at the state level through the Vidhan Sabha, the Vidhan Parishad and the three Lists, and the chapter closes on the challenges of absenteeism, disruption and low productivity, and on the citizen's part in answering them.

scope_in.item: State that after independence the drafting of the Constitution was the first important step in the new epoch, and that it laid foundational principles including Universal Adult Franchise, which guarantees all adult citizens the right to vote irrespective of social or economic background, gender, race or religion

Explain that the people directly elect the representatives who become members of the Lok Sabha, that a majority group from among them forms the government, and that the government can therefore be seen as functioning with the people's consent

Describe the Parliament as the supreme legislative body that makes laws for the country, comprises all elected and nominated representatives of the people, and controls and guides the work of the government
Recall that there have been 17 Lok Sabhas since the first one in 1952 and that the 18th Lok Sabha was constituted in June 2024

Distinguish the old Parliament building, now called Samvidhan Sadan, built in the 1920s, where the Constituent Assembly met for its deliberations and which served as Parliament House for over seven decades, from the new Sansad Bhavan built to accommodate growing needs of capacity, technology, sustainability and safety

Describe the features of the new Parliament building as the students notice them: a three-sided design reflecting balance, inclusivity and purpose, green construction cutting electricity use by 30 per cent, walls carved with peacocks, lotuses, tribal art, temple patterns and freedom fighters, and the Ashokan emblem

Name the parts of the Indian Parliament -- the President and two Houses, the Lok Sabha (House of the People or Lower House) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States or Upper House) -- and explain that a two-House structure is called bicameral, from 'bi' meaning two and 'cameral' meaning chamber or house

State that Lok Sabha members are chosen by direct election based on universal adult suffrage, that the Constitution envisages a maximum of 550 members for this House, that Rajya Sabha MPs are elected indirectly by the electoral college studied in the previous chapter, and that both the Rajya Sabha seats allocated and the Lok Sabha MPs represented are based on the population of each state

Explain why the Constitution makers chose a bicameral system: a single directly elected House was felt to be inadequate for the challenges independent India would face, and in the spirit of federalism a Council of States was needed, with a different composition and a different process of election

Define federalism as a form of government where power is distributed between the centre, the states and local governments, and say that it helps keep the balance between national unity and local interests

List what the chapter gives as the roots of India's parliamentary system: inspiration from Britain's system, the practical experience freedom fighters and Constitution makers gained in British colonial governance structures, the memory of the ancient republics or mahajanapadas, and village panchayats where elders made collective decisions

State that each House has a presiding officer, that Lok Sabha members elect a Speaker who conducts sessions, allows members to speak, maintains discipline and ensures that rules are followed, and that the Vice President of India presides over the Rajya Sabha as its chairperson

Describe the Sengol as a gold-plated silver sceptre handed symbolically to Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru on 14 August 1947 to mark the transfer of power, now placed near the Speaker's chair in the new Lok Sabha, dating back to the Chola period, given to new rulers as a reminder that power must be guided by dharma and righteousness, with Nandi at its top symbolising justice

State that simultaneous interpretation of Parliamentary discussions was earlier available in 12 Indian languages and that six more -- Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Manipuri, Urdu and Sanskrit -- were recently added, with more expected in future

Distinguish the Parliament's 'legislative' function, the making of laws, from its 'executive' responsibility, ensuring that laws are implemented and enforced, and state that the Union Executive gives life to the legislative functions and power of the Parliament

Name the three components of the Union Executive -- the President, the Vice President, and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister -- and state that the Council of Ministers is chosen from among the MPs of both Houses and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha
List the four heads under which the Constitution's key functions of the Parliament are classified: constitutional functions, lawmaking, executive accountability and financial accountability
Give the election of the President and Vice President, and amendments to the Constitution, as constitutional functions of the Parliament, and note that other such functions are left to higher grades

State the four core constitutional values the Parliament is entrusted with upholding: enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage, following the separation of powers between legislature, executive and judiciary, ensuring federalism, and upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies
Define a bill as a draft of a proposed law that needs Parliament's approval before it can be enacted into law, and an act as the instrument through which a law is generally brought into force

Retell the journey of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009: roots in the Directive Principles of State Policy, the argument in court in the early 1990s that it was part of the Right to Life, the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 mandating as Article 21A free and compulsory education for children between 6 and 14 years, tabling as a bill in the Rajya Sabha six years later, a committee's study and suggested modifications, the major debate over funding, and passage in the Lok Sabha with the President's assent in August 2009

Put the steps of lawmaking in order from Fig. 6.8: introduction in either House of the Parliament, reading of the bill, referral to a Standing Committee, taken up for consideration and passing, clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted, vote on the bill, the process repeated in the other House, presidential assent, and gazette notification -- noting the caution that all bills may not be referred to committees
Explain the terms reading, with its origin in the British Parliament where a clerk read the bill out for illiterate MPs, clause, gazette and standing committee

State that some bills, such as a Money Bill concerned with financial matters including taxation and government borrowing, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and that the introduction requires the prior recommendation of the President

Describe the responsibilities of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers as part of the Union Executive: implementing and enforcing laws, overseeing the effective running of the government, taking day-to-day decisions on the principles laid out in the Constitution and its laws, and being answerable to the Lok Sabha

Explain the Question Hour as a select period, typically the first hour of a Parliamentary session, when MPs may ask ministers about government policies and activities, and say how it and special committees that may include MPs from different political parties hold the Executive accountable, that is, make it justify all its actions and decisions
Read an extract from a Standing Committee report and identify who is reporting to whom, the subject reviewed, the Committee's recommendation and the government's action taken

Give the chapter's examples of verse and humour in Parliament: the Tirukkural couplet recited by Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman while presenting the Union Budget for 2025-26 on 1 February 2025, and the exchange of poetic lines between Sushma Swaraj and Dr. Manmohan Singh in the Lok Sabha in 2011

Explain financial accountability: the Parliament approves and monitors government expenditure through the annual budget and by examining the distribution of funds to different ministries, and the government is expected to provide it information in a timely and accurate manner

Describe the President as the Head of State and the nominal head of the Executive who appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers, summons the Parliament and gives assent to bills, is aided and advised by the Council of Ministers, and may exercise discretionary powers in specific circumstances such as when no party holds a clear majority in a Lok Sabha election

Describe the Prime Minister as the de facto executive authority, appointed by the President as leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha and serving with the support of a majority of Lok Sabha MPs, and list the key functions of leading the Council of Ministers, advising the President, coordinating the work of different ministries and shaping national policies

State that the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, that most bills that come to the Parliament are initiated by the government, and that a permanent group of officials called civil servants, also called administrators or bureaucrats, work under the direction of ministers to implement laws and policies

Use Lal Bahadur Shastri's resignation as Railway Minister in 1956 after a train accident, though he was not blamed for it, to explain a minister taking moral responsibility for anything that happens in their ministry

Compare the Legislature and the Executive on composition, main role and functions using the table: who may introduce bills and who introduces most of them, who asks questions and who provides explanations, who sanctions government-related expenses and who prepares and implements the budget, and who consults Parliamentary committees

Describe the Judiciary as the branch that interprets and applies the laws of the land, functions through a system of courts, acts as the custodian of the Constitution, checks that laws passed by Parliament do not violate the Constitutional framework, and can step in when a violation occurs while the Executive implements a law
Explain separation of powers and the system of checks and balances among the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary as the arrangement that ensures no one organ becomes too powerful
State that each state has its own legislature and executive called its State Assembly, and that Members of Legislative Assembly formulate laws on subjects in the State List and the Concurrent List

Explain the Union List, the State List and the Concurrent List, that both the Union and the state governments may legislate on Concurrent List subjects, that a state is bound to follow the Union if the Union legislates on such a subject, and that RTE applies all over India although education is in the Concurrent List

Compare the union and state structures using the parallel-structure table: the President elected by an electoral college against the Governor appointed by the President, five-year terms, the nominal head against the de facto executive head, selection of the leader of the majority party or coalition, who selects the Council of Ministers, collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha or the Vidhan Sabha, bicameral against possibly unicameral legislatures, the lower and upper Houses, the Speaker as presiding officer, legislative powers over the respective Lists, and where money bills originate

State that state legislatures may be unicameral with one house or bicameral with two, name the Vidhan Sabha as the legislative assembly and the Vidhan Parishad as the legislative council, and name the six states with a bicameral system: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh

List the roles of the Indian legislature, including the Parliament and the State Assemblies: enacting laws, overseeing administrative processes, approving the budget, providing a platform for discussing national policies, development plans and international relations, and addressing public grievances

Name the challenges to the effective functioning of the legislatures: regular absenteeism of members, non-cooperative conduct or communication of members, reduced quality of important debates, and disruptions of the Question Hour

State that the Parliament typically meets three times a year in Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions, that each session has sittings where the Parliament deliberates on proposed laws, discusses governance and seeks explanations from the Executive, that it usually sits for 6 hours a day which may be extended, and that the State Assemblies follow similar schedules

Define productivity in the Parliamentary context as the hours a House actually functioned measured against the time it was scheduled to, and draw conclusions from M. Venkaiah Naidu's 2021 statement about the Rajya Sabha's productivity falling from about 78 per cent in 2004-14 to about 65 per cent, and to its lowest recorded 35.75 per cent in 2018
Draw conclusions about the functioning of Parliament over time from the table of sessions and sittings of the 1st, 2nd, 10th and 13th Lok Sabhas

State the concerns expressed by sections of society that a substantial proportion of Lok Sabha representatives have criminal cases against them and that many sessions are marked by angry or biased debates that do not seriously address people's issues, and note the media's role in communicating the concerns of the electorate, including with humour

Explain how informed and engaged citizens strengthen democracy by asking questions, sharing views, participating in public debate including on the digital spaces government departments offer during policymaking, and constructively engaging with political representatives on policies

Summarise the chapter's closing points: power is shared, decisions are debated and leaders are held accountable; the Legislature makes laws, the Executive implements them and the Judiciary ensures they follow the Constitution; structures at the Centre and in the states balance representation, responsibility and unity; and the functioning of Parliament needs to become more efficient and productive

concepts.name: Parliament in India's democracy: the Constitution, universal franchise and the two buildings
concepts.description: How independence led to the Constitution and Universal Adult Franchise, how the directly elected Lok Sabha produces a government that rests on the people's consent, what makes the Parliament the supreme legislative body, and what the students notice about the old and new Parliament buildings.
concepts.idea: A free country had to decide how it would govern itself, and the answer it wrote down was a Parliament that every adult citizen helps to choose.
concepts.rule: India's independence was won through great sacrifices, and the first important step of the new epoch was drafting the Constitution, which laid foundational principles including Universal Adult Franchise -- the right of every adult citizen to vote irrespective of social or economic background, gender, race or religion. The people directly elect the representatives who become members of the Lok Sabha, and a majority group from among them forms the government, so the government functions with the people's consent. The Parliament is the supreme legislative body: it makes laws for the country, comprises all elected and nominated representatives of the people, and controls and guides the work of the government. There have been 17 Lok Sabhas since the first in 1952, and the 18th was constituted in June 2024.
concepts.example: The old Parliament building, now called Samvidhan Sadan, was constructed in the 1920s, hosted the Constituent Assembly's deliberations and served as Parliament House for over seven decades; the new Sansad Bhavan was built to accommodate growing needs of capacity, technology, sustainability and safety, with a three-sided design reflecting balance, inclusivity and purpose, green construction that cuts electricity use by 30 per cent, and walls carved with peacocks, lotuses, tribal art, temple patterns and freedom fighters.

questions.q: A visitor leaves the new Parliament building saying, 'It feels like a museum of India.' Using only what this chapter tells you, set out what makes that a fair description and what makes it an incomplete one.
questions.a: It is fair because the building houses so many ancient symbols: the walls carry carvings of peacocks, lotuses, tribal art, temple patterns and freedom fighters, and the Ashokan emblem stands in it, so a visitor moves past centuries of Indian imagery. It is incomplete because a museum only preserves, while this is a working House built for growing needs of capacity, technology, sustainability and safety, using green construction that cuts electricity use by 30 per cent. The chapter's own answer is that democracy must look ahead but never forget its roots, and the building is meant to do both at once.
s: Names museum-like features such as the carvings of peacocks, lotuses, tribal art, temple patterns and freedom fighters, or the Ashokan emblem
Notes that these are ancient symbols housed in a newly built building
Argues the other side using the building's working purpose -- capacity, technology, sustainability and safety, or its green construction saving 30 per cent of electricity
Concludes with the chapter's point that democracy must look ahead but never forget its roots

questions.q: Why does it matter that the right to vote is guaranteed irrespective of social or economic background, gender, race or religion? Explain what would be lost if any one of those conditions were allowed to bar a citizen.
questions.a: It means that no adult citizen can be kept out of the vote on any of these grounds, so every section of society has a share in choosing the representatives. If even one ground were allowed to bar people, a whole group would have no voice in the Lok Sabha, and the government formed by the majority of those representatives could no longer be said to rest on the consent of all the people.
s: States that no adult citizen can be excluded from voting on any of these grounds
Explains that every section of society therefore has a say in choosing representatives
Draws the consequence that barring a group would leave it voiceless, so the government would no longer rest on the whole people's consent

questions.q: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar told the Constituent Assembly in November 1949 that the Constitution 'is not a mere lawyer's document; it is a vehicle of life, and its spirit is always the spirit of the age.' Using the Introduction to this chapter, explain what he might have meant.
questions.a: A mere lawyer's document would be only a set of rules to be argued over in court. The Constitution is more than that: it was the first important step of a new epoch, and it laid the foundational principles of the whole nation, such as Universal Adult Franchise. It is a vehicle of life because it is what carries ordinary citizens' decisions into real governance -- their votes elect the Lok Sabha, and the majority among those members forms the government. Saying its spirit is the spirit of the age suggests it must keep answering the needs of each period, which is what the chapter means when it says democracy must look ahead while never forgetting its roots.
s: Explains what a mere lawyer's document would be -- rules to be read and argued in court
Says the Constitution instead laid the foundational principles of the nation, including Universal Adult Franchise
Explains 'vehicle of life' by the way citizens' votes are carried into a government that governs them
Explains 'spirit of the age' as the Constitution having to keep meeting the needs of each period

concepts.name: A bicameral Parliament: the two Houses, why India chose two, and who presides
concepts.description: The composition of the Indian Parliament as the President with the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, what bicameral means, how each House is filled, the roots of India's parliamentary system, the federal reasoning behind the Council of States, the presiding officers of the two Houses, and the symbols and languages of the House.
concepts.idea: India did not settle for one House of directly elected members, because a country of many states needed a second chamber to speak for the states themselves.
concepts.rule: The Indian Parliament is composed of the President and two houses: the Lok Sabha, the House of the People or Lower House, and the Rajya Sabha, the Council of States or Upper House. A structure with two houses is called bicameral, from 'bi' meaning two and 'cameral' meaning chamber or house. Lok Sabha members are chosen by direct election based on universal adult suffrage, and the Constitution envisages a maximum of 550 members for this House; Rajya Sabha MPs are elected indirectly by an electoral college. Both the number of Rajya Sabha seats allocated and the number of Lok Sabha MPs represented are based on the population of each state. Each House has a presiding officer: Lok Sabha members elect a Speaker, and the Vice President of India presides over the Rajya Sabha as its chairperson.
concepts.example: During the making of the Constitution it was felt that a single directly elected House would be inadequate for the challenges independent India would face, and that in the spirit of federalism -- power distributed between the centre, the states and local governments -- a Council of States was needed, with its composition and process of election deliberately designed to be different.

questions.q: Two small states have very different populations. Using what the chapter says about how each House is filled, explain what each House would look like for them, and what the second House is meant to add.
questions.a: In the Lok Sabha the number of MPs a state has is based on its population, and those members are directly elected by the people under universal adult suffrage, so the more populous state would send more members and would count for more in that House. Rajya Sabha seats are also allocated on the basis of population, but its members are elected indirectly by an electoral college and its composition and process of election were deliberately designed to be different. The second House was added in the spirit of federalism, as a Council of States, because it was felt that a single directly elected House would be inadequate for the challenges independent India would face; its purpose is to keep the balance between national unity and the interests of the states.
s: States that Lok Sabha membership for a state follows its population and that those members are directly elected

questions.q: Why might it matter that the two Houses have different presiding officers -- one elected from among the members, the other holding a separate constitutional office?
questions.a: In the Lok Sabha the members elect the Speaker from among themselves, so the person who conducts the sessions, allows members to speak and maintains discipline holds the chair by the confidence of the House itself. In the Rajya Sabha the chair is held by the Vice President of India, who is not one of its elected members, so the Council of States is presided over by someone standing a little outside the House. The difference fits the different character of the two Houses, since the Rajya Sabha's composition and process of election were also deliberately designed to be different.
s: States that the Lok Sabha elects its Speaker from among its own members

questions.q: 'The memory of the mahajanapadas and of village panchayats is as much a root of our Parliament as Britain is.' Examine this claim using what the chapter says, and say how far you agree.
questions.a: The chapter does treat both as roots. It says plainly that Britain's system inspired our system of parliamentary democracy, and also that the Constitution makers had the memory of the ancient republics, the mahajanapadas, and of village panchayats where elders made collective decisions. It further notes their practical experience of British colonial governance structures, which gave familiarity with parliamentary procedures. The two roots are not identical in kind: Britain supplied the working shape of a parliamentary system, while the Indian memories supplied the older habit of deciding matters collectively. A fair judgement is that the claim is largely right in spirit, because the chapter refuses to present the system as borrowed alone, though it gives Britain the more specific credit for the parliamentary form itself.
s: States that the chapter credits Britain's system as the inspiration for parliamentary democracy
States that the chapter also names the mahajanapadas and village panchayats as roots
Distinguishes the kinds of contribution -- a working parliamentary form against an older habit of collective decision-making
Reaches a judgement and supports it from the chapter rather than from outside it

questions.q: Do you think a country as varied as India is better served by two Houses than by one? Give the strongest reason on each side from this chapter, and state your view.
questions.a: For two Houses: it was felt during the making of the Constitution that a single directly elected House would be inadequate for the challenges independent India would face, and a Council of States was needed in the spirit of federalism to keep the balance between national unity and local interests. Against: the Lok Sabha is the House the people themselves elect directly under universal adult suffrage, so it can be argued that it already carries the people's voice and a second, indirectly elected House adds a further step. A defensible view is that the second House is worth having, because India distributes power between the centre, the states and local governments, and the states need a chamber of their own.
s: Gives the case for two Houses from the inadequacy of a single House and the federal need for a Council of States

concepts.name: The Union Executive and the Parliament's four key functions
concepts.description: The difference between the Parliament's legislative function and its executive responsibility, the three components of the Union Executive and their link to the Lok Sabha, the four heads under which the Constitution's key functions of Parliament are classified, and the constitutional function in particular.
concepts.idea: Making a law is only half the job; someone has to see that it is carried out, and the Constitution puts both halves inside the same system.
concepts.rule: The 'executive' responsibility of the Parliament, ensuring that laws are implemented and enforced, is as important as its 'legislative' function, the making of laws, and the Union Executive gives life to the legislative functions and power of the Parliament. The Union Executive consists of the President, the Vice President, and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. The Council of Ministers is chosen from among the MPs of both houses of Parliament, and these ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. The key functions the Constitution lays down for the Parliament are broadly classified under four heads: constitutional functions, lawmaking, executive accountability and financial accountability.
concepts.example: Constitutional functions include the election of the President and the Vice President and amendments to the Constitution; under this head the Parliament is entrusted with upholding core values -- enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage, following the separation of powers between legislature, executive and judiciary, ensuring federalism, and upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies.

questions.q: The chapter lists upholding the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles of State Policy as one core value entrusted to the Parliament, and says it does this 'by framing laws and policies'. Analyse why that last phrase matters, using another part of the chapter as evidence.
questions.a: The phrase matters because it says how the Parliament upholds these values: not by declaring them, but by turning them into laws and policies that actually reach people. The chapter's own evidence is the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act. Its roots lay in the Directive Principles of State Policy, and the Constitution makers had wanted it implemented within a decade of Independence; because no law was framed, countless children were left without access to education. Only when the Parliament acted -- the amendment of 2002 and then the Act of 2009 -- did the principle become something that created legal pathways for children to attend school. The example shows that a value left unframed changes nothing, which is exactly why the duty is stated as framing laws and policies.

concepts.name: Lawmaking: from bill to act, and the journey of the RTE
concepts.description: What a bill and an act are, the elaborate process by which a bill becomes an act, the vocabulary of reading, clause, gazette and standing committee, the special case of the Money Bill, and the long journey of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.
concepts.idea: A law does not appear the day someone thinks of it; it has to survive a long, deliberate journey through both Houses before it can bind anybody.
concepts.rule: Among the primary responsibilities of the legislature is to make laws, and the Constitution has laid out an elaborate and rigorous process for doing it. A law is generally brought into force through an instrument called an act. A bill is a draft of a proposed law that needs to be approved by the Parliament before it can be enacted into law. The steps shown in Fig. 6.8 run: introduction in either House of the Parliament, reading of the bill, referral to a Standing Committee, taken up for consideration and passing, clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted, vote on the bill, the process repeated in the other House, presidential assent, and gazette notification. The chapter cautions that all bills may not be referred to committees.
concepts.example: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act came into existence in August 2009, though the idea began almost a century before: its roots lay in the Directive Principles of State Policy, an argument was made in court in the early 1990s that it was part of the Right to Life, the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 mandated it as Article 21A for children between 6 and 14 years, it was tabled as a bill in the Rajya Sabha six years later, a committee studied it and suggested modifications, the major debate concerned funding, and in August 2009 it was passed in the Lok Sabha and received the President's assent.

questions.q: Retell the journey of the RTE from an idea to an act, keeping the stages in order and naming what happened at each.
questions.a: Its roots lay in the Directive Principles of State Policy, and the Constitution makers had wanted it implemented within a decade after Independence, which did not happen, leaving countless children without access to education. Parliamentary action began some years later with the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002, which mandated as Article 21A that the state shall provide free and compulsory education to all children between 6 and 14 years. Six years later the bill was tabled in the Rajya Sabha, a committee studied it thoroughly and suggested modifications, and the major debate concerned funding, since new schools, infrastructure and teachers for millions of children would be costly. By 2008 the MPs determined that it was time; after the 2009 elections the new government pursued the matter, and in August 2009 the bill was passed in the Lok Sabha and received the President's assent, becoming an Act.

A single vote on the whole bill would force members to accept or reject every detail together, and a wrong detail could pass simply because the rest of the bill was good.

questions.a: The first delay was that a principle was written down but not enacted: RTE's roots lay in the Directive Principles, and although the Constitution makers wanted it implemented within a decade after Independence, no law was framed, leaving countless children without access to education. The second stage was not a delay of neglect but of argument: in the early 1990s the case was made in court that education was part of the Right to Life, and it took until 2002 for Parliament to act through the 86th Constitutional Amendment. The hardest to avoid was the funding debate, because that question could not be settled by goodwill alone; the first delay is the least defensible, since nothing was being weighed at all.

Against: a Standing Committee is a permanent body of MPs that scrutinises and asks questions, and in the case of RTE a committee studied the bill thoroughly and suggested modifications, so skipping that stage loses a careful reading the House itself may not have time for. A reasonable judgement is that the committee stage should be the normal course and skipping it the exception, because the cost of a poorly examined law lasts far longer than the delay.

concepts.name: Holding the government to account: executive and financial accountability
concepts.description: How the Parliament makes the Executive justify itself -- the responsibilities of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the Question Hour, committees that question ministries, a real Standing Committee report, and the Parliament's control of the public purse through the annual budget.
concepts.idea: The people cannot question a minister themselves, so the House they elected does it for them, in the open and on the record.
concepts.rule: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are part of the Union Executive. They are primarily responsible for implementing and enforcing laws and overseeing the effective running of the government; they take decisions on the day-to-day functioning of the government based on the principles laid out in the Constitution and its laws; and they are answerable to the Lok Sabha through mechanisms like the Question Hour, a select period, typically the first hour of a Parliamentary session, where MPs may ask ministers questions about government policies and activities. To be accountable means that the Executive must justify all its actions and decisions. Under financial accountability the Parliament approves and monitors government expenditure through the annual budget and by examining the distribution of funds to different ministries.

Third, MPs can raise it in the Question Hour, the select period where they may ask ministers about government policies and activities, which requires the minister to justify her actions and decisions. questions.q: Why might it matter that committees questioning a ministry include MPs from different political parties?
questions.a: The ministers belong to the majority group that formed the government, so questions coming only from their own side might be gentle or might never be asked. A committee drawn from different political parties brings in members who have no stake in defending the ministry, so the questions are more likely to be searching. It also makes the scrutiny harder to dismiss as one party's complaint, since the recommendation carries members from more than one side, which is what makes it a scrutiny of the government rather than a quarrel between parties.

questions.q: 'Executive accountability and financial accountability are really the same duty wearing two coats.' Examine this claim using the chapter, and reach a conclusion.
questions.a: There is real force in the claim. Both are ways the Parliament makes the Executive answer for what it has done: under executive accountability ministers must justify their actions and decisions, and under financial accountability they must show how public money has been spent. Both depend on the government supplying information, and both can be pursued through the same forums -- the Question Hour and committees. But the chapter lists them as separate heads, and the difference is real: executive accountability is about decisions and conduct, and can be exercised at any moment during a session, while financial accountability works through a particular instrument, the annual budget, and a particular examination, the distribution of funds to different ministries, which happens on a fixed cycle and grants or withholds the means to act at all. The conclusion is that they share a purpose but not a method, so the two coats are worth keeping distinct.
s: Sets out what the two heads have in common -- making the Executive answer, and depending on information from it

concepts.name: The Executive at work, and how it differs from the Legislature
concepts.description: The President as Head of State and nominal head of the Executive, the Prime Minister as the de facto authority and the Council of Ministers, the civil servants who carry policy into departments, moral responsibility in office, and the point-by-point difference between the Legislature and the Executive.
concepts.idea: India has a head of state and a head of government, and knowing which one actually decides is the key to reading the whole system.
concepts.rule: The President is the Head of State and the nominal head of the Executive: the President appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers, summons the Parliament and gives assent to bills, and the Council of Ministers aids and advises the President, though in specific circumstances -- particularly political crises, such as when no party holds a clear majority in a Lok Sabha election -- the President can exercise discretionary powers. The Prime Minister is the de facto executive authority: the President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister, who serves with the support of the majority of MPs in that House. The Prime Minister's key functions are leading the Council of Ministers, advising the President, coordinating the work of different ministries, and shaping national policies.
concepts.example: In 1956 the Railway Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned after a train accident; although he was not blamed for it, he believed a minister must take moral responsibility for anything that happens in their ministry, and although Prime Minister Nehru declined the resignation at first, Shastri insisted and it was finally accepted.

questions.q: Part V of the Constitution begins with Chapter I, The Executive, and only then in Chapter II sets out the role and functions of Parliament. The chapter asks why this might be so. Give a reasoned answer.
questions.a: One reading is that the Constitution first establishes who will hold the offices of state -- the President, the Vice President and the Council of Ministers -- because these are the offices through which the union acts at all, and only then describes the body that makes the laws they will carry out. A second reading is that it reflects the relationship the chapter describes: the Union Executive is what gives life to the legislative functions and power of the Parliament, so the Constitution names the organ that will act before the organ that will instruct it. A third is simply that the President, who is part of the Executive, is also part of the Parliament and must be introduced before the Parliament can be described. The chapter leaves the question open, and any of these answers is defensible provided it is argued from the relationship between the two organs rather than from the order being accidental.

Uses the relationship between the organs, such as the Executive giving life to the Parliament's legislative power

questions.a: For: he believed a minister must take moral responsibility for anything that happens in their ministry, and a minister who answers only for personal fault leaves the ministry itself answerable to nobody, which sits badly with a Council of Ministers that is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Against: he was not at fault, the Prime Minister declined the resignation at first, and losing a capable minister does not repair an accident or improve the railways. A defensible judgement is that he was right, because the standard he set makes accountability a matter of office rather than of personal blame, and that standard outlasts any single minister.

concepts.name: The Judiciary and the system of checks and balances
concepts.description: The Judiciary as the branch that interprets and applies the laws, its work as custodian of the Constitution over both the Legislature and the Executive, and the separation of powers and checks and balances that keep any one organ from becoming too powerful.
concepts.idea: Two organs make and carry out the law; a third exists to ask whether either of them has stepped outside the Constitution.
concepts.rule: The Judiciary is the branch of government responsible for interpreting and applying the laws of the land, including in specific cases of disputes. It functions through a system of courts and acts as the custodian of the Constitution, ensuring that all branches of the government operate within the principles and parameters enshrined in it. It keeps a check on the functioning of society and the institutions of government by interpreting laws, resolving disputes and safeguarding fundamental rights. It is given the unique and critical responsibility of checking that the laws passed by Parliament have not violated the Constitutional framework, and if a violation occurs when laws are implemented by the Executive, the Judiciary again has the power to step in.
concepts.example: Just as the Parliament functions through its Legislature and Executive arms, the Judiciary functions through its Courts; together these arrangements are the separation of powers and the system of checks and balances among the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary, which ensure that no one organ becomes too powerful.

questions.q: The chapter asks what might happen if one organ had all the power, and how that could affect the rights of people. Answer it, working through each organ in turn.
questions.a: If the Legislature held all the power, the laws it passed could not be tested against the Constitutional framework, so it could pass a law taking away a fundamental right and nobody would be placed to say otherwise. If the Executive held all the power, it would both carry out the laws and decide whether it had carried them out properly, so a violation committed during implementation would never be reached; the Question Hour and the sanctioning of expenses would become empty, because nobody could compel an answer. If the Judiciary held all the power, it would interpret rules it had itself made and there would be no elected body to answer to the people, so the arrangement would no longer rest on the people's consent. In every case rights suffer, because rights are protected not by any one organ's goodwill but by the fact that each is watched by another -- which is why the chapter says checks and balances exist so that no one organ becomes too powerful.
s: Works out the danger of the Legislature holding all power, using laws unchecked against the Constitution

questions.q: Why is it significant that the Judiciary's check reaches both the making of a law and the carrying out of a law?
questions.a: A check on making alone would let a perfectly constitutional law be applied in a way that breaks the Constitution, and officials could do through implementation what the law itself never authorised. A check on implementation alone would leave the law itself untouchable, so a provision that violated the Constitutional framework would stand however carefully it was applied. Because the Judiciary reaches both, there is no stage at which an organ can act outside the Constitution unexamined, which is what makes it the custodian of the Constitution rather than merely a court of disputes.

The honest conclusion is that the chapter's logic requires some review to exist, but this chapter does not say what it is.

For: the Constitution is what the people gave themselves, and it lists the specific responsibilities of each organ; the Judiciary is not substituting its own preference but checking that a law has not violated the Constitutional framework, and it safeguards fundamental rights that a passing majority could otherwise remove. A defensible judgement is that the power is right precisely because it is limited to that question, and because without it the promise of checks and balances would be empty.

concepts.name: Legislature and executive at the state level: the Lists and the parallel structure
concepts.description: How each state has its own legislature and executive, the Union, State and Concurrent Lists that divide what each may legislate on, the point-by-point parallel between the union and state structures, and the unicameral or bicameral shape of state legislatures.
concepts.idea: The structure at the state level imitates the one at the union level, which is what makes federalism workable rather than merely a word.
concepts.rule: Each state has its own legislature and executive, called its State Assembly. Just as the Parliament has Members of Parliament who make laws, there are Members of Legislative Assembly who formulate laws on subjects on the State List and the Concurrent List. The Constitution has lists clarifying the areas on which the Union and State governments can exclusively legislate -- the Union List and the State List -- and a Concurrent List of subjects on which both may legislate; if the Union government legislates on a Concurrent List subject, the state government is bound to follow it. Unlike the Centre, state legislatures can be unicameral, having only one house, or bicameral, having two: the legislative assembly is the Vidhan Sabha and the legislative council, the upper house, is the Vidhan Parishad.
concepts.example: The RTE Act applies all over India even though education is in the Concurrent List; and the states with a bicameral system are Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh, while the remaining states have a unicameral system.

Matters of this kind require collaboration between the Union and the states, because a policy made only at one level would not reach or would not suit the whole country. That is interdependence rather than separation: federalism here is not each government working in its own sealed area but the two having to work on the same subject together, which is what keeps the balance between national unity and local interests.

questions.q: 'The structure at the state level imitates the one at the union level.' Test this statement against the table, setting out where the imitation is exact and where it is not.
questions.a: The imitation is close in most rows. Both levels have a constitutional head with a five-year term; both distinguish a nominal head from a de facto executive authority; in both, the executive head is the leader of the majority party or coalition in the lower House and selects the Council of Ministers; in both, that council is collectively responsible to the lower House; both lower Houses have a five-year term and a Speaker; and in both, money bills originate only in the lower House. The imitation is not exact in two places. First, the constitutional heads arrive differently: the President is elected by an electoral college, while the Governor is appointed by the President, so the state's head owes the office to the union rather than to an election. Second, the legislature's shape differs: the Parliament is always bicameral, but a state legislature may be unicameral with only a Vidhan Sabha, since the Vidhan Parishad exists in some states only. The statement is therefore sound as a general description, but the manner of appointing the Governor is a real asymmetry, not a variation.

questions.q: Should more states adopt a second house, the Vidhan Parishad? Argue a case using the reasoning the chapter gives for the Rajya Sabha.
questions.a: For: the reasoning that produced the Rajya Sabha was that a single directly elected House would be inadequate for the challenges the country faced, and that a second chamber with a different composition adds a further reading before a law is settled; a state facing complex laws might gain the same benefit. Against: only six states have one and the rest manage with a unicameral legislature, so a second house is clearly not necessary for a state to function, and it adds cost and delay to lawmaking. A defensible judgement is that it should be a state's own choice, which fits federalism, where power is distributed and local interests are allowed to differ.

concepts.name: Challenges to the effective functioning of the legislatures, and the citizen's role
concepts.description: What the Indian legislature is meant to do, the challenges of absenteeism, disruption and declining productivity, how sessions and sittings are organised, what the data on sessions, sittings and productivity shows, and how informed and engaged citizens strengthen a democracy.
concepts.idea: A legislature that does not sit, or sits without debating, cannot do any of the work the Constitution gave it -- and the remedy begins with citizens who are paying attention.
concepts.rule: The Indian legislature, including the Parliament at the Centre and the State Assemblies, has the critical role of enacting laws, overseeing administrative processes and approving the budget, and it provides a platform for discussing national policies, development plans and international relations and for addressing public grievances. Its challenges include regular absenteeism of members, non-cooperative conduct or communication of members, reduced quality of important debates, and disruptions of the Question Hour. The Parliament typically meets three times a year in Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions, each with sittings, and usually sits for 6 hours a day, which can be extended on special occasions or for urgent business; the State Assemblies have similar schedules.
concepts.example: In the Parliamentary context productivity is measured by the hours a House actually functioned against the time it was scheduled to; M. Venkaiah Naidu stated in 2021 that the Rajya Sabha's productivity had been about 78 per cent during 2004-14 and had declined to about 65 per cent since, with 2018 recording the lowest ever at 35.75 per cent under the impact of disruptions.

questions.q: What conclusions can be drawn from the table of sessions and sittings of the 1st, 2nd, 10th and 13th Lok Sabhas?
questions.a: The number of sessions has stayed roughly steady, between 14 and 16 across all four. The number of sittings, however, has fallen sharply: 677 in the 1st Lok Sabha and 567 in the 2nd, against 423 in the 10th and 356 in the 13th. So the Parliament has continued to meet about as often, but it has met for far fewer days within those sessions, which means less time for the deliberation, discussion and seeking of explanations that sittings exist for.

questions.q: What conclusions can be drawn from M. Venkaiah Naidu's 2021 statement, and what does it imply for the role the Rajya Sabha is expected to play?
questions.a: It shows a clear decline: the Rajya Sabha's productivity was about 78 per cent during 2004-14 and fell to about 65 per cent afterwards, and of the eleven sessions he presided over, four fell to very low figures, with 2018 recording the lowest ever at 35.75 per cent under the impact of disruptions. Since productivity measures the hours a House actually functioned against the hours it was scheduled to, the implication is that for much of its scheduled time the House was not working at all. The Rajya Sabha was created in the spirit of federalism as a Council of States to add a second, considered reading; a House sitting for barely a third of its scheduled time cannot perform that role, so the decline undercuts the very reason it exists.

Explains what those figures mean, given that productivity measures functioning hours against scheduled hours

questions.q: A bill that many people are waiting for has still not been discussed after two sessions. Using this chapter, explain the ways in which the legislature's difficulties could have produced this, and what it costs.
questions.a: Several of the named challenges could produce it. Regular absenteeism of members can leave the House without the presence a serious debate needs. Non-cooperative conduct or communication of members and disruptions can stop business altogether, which is what low productivity measures: the Rajya Sabha functioned for as little as 35.75 per cent of its scheduled time in 2018. The fall in sittings compounds it, since the number of sittings dropped from 677 in the 1st Lok Sabha to 356 in the 13th, so there are fewer days in which anything can be taken up. The cost is set out by the chapter: the Parliament and the State Assemblies were envisioned as spaces for thoughtful debates where laws are made in the interest of the people, and when debates are disrupted, sessions are cut short and bills take years to be passed, it becomes a matter of concern -- both because the law people are waiting for does not arrive, and because it weakens the trust people place in their representatives.

Uses the productivity idea or a figure to show scheduled time not being used
Uses the decline in the number of sittings as a compounding cause
States the cost in the chapter's own terms -- laws delayed, and trust in representatives weakened

questions.q: Why does the chapter treat disruption of the Question Hour as a distinct and serious challenge, rather than as one disruption among many?
questions.a: The Question Hour is the mechanism through which the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are answerable to the Lok Sabha: it is the select period when MPs may ask ministers about government policies and activities and require them to justify their actions and decisions. Disrupting it does not merely waste an hour; it removes the occasion on which the Executive is made accountable at all. Other business can usually be taken up later, but a question not asked is an explanation never demanded, so this particular disruption strikes at one of the four key functions the Constitution gives the Parliament.

Explains that disrupting it removes the occasion for holding the Executive accountable

questions.q: Atal Bihari Vajpayee told the Lok Sabha that governments will come and go and parties will rise and fall, but the nation must endure and its democracy must live on. Analyse what this says about the role of Parliament and its leaders, and why it matters that democratic values are protected even when political power changes.
questions.a: The remark separates two things that are easily confused: the people who hold power at a given moment, and the institution through which power is held. Governments and parties are temporary -- the chapter itself counts eighteen Lok Sabhas since 1952 -- while the Parliament, the Constitution and the democracy they serve are meant to outlast all of them. For leaders, this implies that their duty is to the institution rather than to their own side: a minister answers to the Lok Sabha, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to it, and the Parliament is expected to remain a space for thoughtful debate whichever party is in a majority. It matters that values are protected across changes of power because the checks that protect citizens -- questioning, accountability, the Judiciary's guardianship of the Constitution -- are only worth anything if they survive a change of government; a check that the winning side can set aside is no check at all. The chapter's own remedy points the same way: citizens who stay informed and engaged are what keeps the institution stronger than whoever currently occupies it.
s: Distinguishes temporary governments and parties from the enduring institution and democracy
Draws out what this means for leaders, such as duty to the institution or answerability to the House
Explains why protection across changes of power matters, using checks that must survive a change of government
Connects to the chapter's remedy of informed and engaged citizens, or to its concern for Parliament's functioning

questions.q: The chapter says one of the best ways to overcome these challenges is for many more citizens to stay informed and engaged. Judge whether that is a sufficient remedy.
questions.a: In its favour: the chapter's whole argument is that representatives answer to the people, so citizens who ask questions, share views, take part in public debate on the digital spaces government departments offer during policymaking, and engage constructively with representatives change what a representative can get away with; the chapter also notes that more young leaders and diverse voices are entering public life and that technology makes involvement easier. Against: it puts the burden on those with the least power, and it does nothing directly about absenteeism, disruption or the fall in sittings, which are matters of how the House itself is run. A reasonable judgement is that it is necessary but not sufficient -- essential as the pressure behind any reform, but needing changes inside the House to go with it.
s: Gives the case for, using the citizen actions the chapter names
Gives the case against, noting that it does not directly address absenteeism, disruption or fewer sittings
Reaches a judgement, such as necessary but not sufficient, and supports it

questions.q: Your class is preparing a one-minute address to be read in a school assembly, titled 'Why a quiet Parliament should worry us'. Draft its four main points.
questions.a: A reasonable draft. First, the Parliament is not a building but a job: it enacts laws, oversees administrative processes, approves the budget, and gives the country a place to discuss its policies and grievances. Second, that job needs time, and the time is shrinking -- the 1st Lok Sabha had 677 sittings, the 13th only 356, although the number of sessions barely changed. Third, when the House is disrupted its scheduled hours go unused; the Rajya Sabha functioned for only 35.75 per cent of its scheduled time in 2018, and a disrupted Question Hour means ministers are never made to justify their decisions. Fourth, the remedy is not only theirs but ours: citizens who stay informed, ask questions, join public discussion on the digital platforms departments open during policymaking, and engage constructively with their representatives, make it costlier to waste the House's time -- and as future voters, we are the pressure behind that change.
s: Opens by stating what the legislature's work actually is
Uses data on sittings or sessions to show the shrinking of time
Uses disruption or productivity, and explains the specific loss of the Question Hour
Ends with the citizen's part, naming actions the chapter gives
